Content:
Recall that a transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}: V \to W] between two vector spaces [MATH: V] and [MATH: W] is linear if for any vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\in V] and any scalar [MATH: k\in\mathbb{R}], the following conditions are satisfied:

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v}_1) = k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)]
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)+\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)]

Content:
It is easy to check that if a transformation can be represented as a matrix, then it is a linear transformation. Therefore, the transformation [MATH: \mathbf{S}] is a linear transformation.

Content:
In general, if [MATH: V] and [MATH: W] are [MATH: n]-dimensional and [MATH: m]-dimensional vector spaces respectively, then the standard matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}\!: V \!\rightarrow W] is an [MATH: m\times n] matrix [MATH: T].

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Similar to transformations in a vector space, we can define a transformation between two different vector spaces. For instance, consider the transformation that maps the vector

[MATH: [x; y]]

from [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] to the vector

Content:
[MATH: [x + y; x − y; 2x + 2y]]

in [MATH: \mathbb{R}^3,] which can be written as

Content:
[MATH: [x; y]]

Content:
The standard matrix of this transformation is

Content:
[MATH: [1|1; 1|− 1; 2|2]]

Content:
Recall that a transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}: V \to W] between two vector spaces [MATH: V] and [MATH: W] is linear if for any vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2\in V] and any scalar [MATH: k\in\mathbb{R}], the following conditions are satisfied:

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(k\mathbf{v}_1) = k\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)]
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)+\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)]

Content:
It is easy to check that if a transformation can be represented as a matrix, then it is a linear transformation. Therefore, the transformation [MATH: \mathbf{S}] is a linear transformation.

Content:
In general, if [MATH: V] and [MATH: W] are [MATH: n]-dimensional and [MATH: m]-dimensional vector spaces respectively, then the standard matrix of a linear transformation [MATH: \mathbf{T}\!: V \!\rightarrow W] is an [MATH: m\times n] matrix [MATH: T].
